criteria.name: Economy with information density
criteria.instruction: Score high when nearly every line advances action, character, atmosphere, or world understanding; score low when passages are removable summary, repetition, or digression.
criteria.rationale: R04 compresses its entire premise into a tightly patterned poem, and R16 delivers a complete moral reversal in very little space.

criteria.name: Control of a sustained, distinct narrative voice
criteria.instruction: Judge whether the story commits to one narrative voice/register and holds it for the whole piece, versus drifting between incompatible registers. High end: a distinctive voice (ironic, confessional, mythic, etc.) sustained from the first line to the last. Low end: the register shifts unpredictably in a way that reads as uncontrolled rather than intentional.
criteria.rationale: R17 sustains an ironic, aphoristic essayistic voice throughout ('the decorative swan... before it has had time to preen itself'); R34 sustains a flat pulp-confessional voice throughout. Contrast R24, which lurches between stoner-comedy profanity and sincere religious sentiment without the shift feeling controlled.

criteria.name: Contradictory inner motives
criteria.instruction: Score high when a character has competing motives that appear in thought, behavior, and consequential choices; score low when characters possess only one stated attitude and never meaningfully conflict with themselves.
criteria.rationale: R02 combines benevolence, guilt, resentment, and self-punishment; R12 makes generosity inseparable from vanity and power.

criteria.name: Embodied sensory and physical grounding
criteria.instruction: Judge how much the story grounds its events in concrete bodily sensation and physical detail (touch, taste, muscle strain, texture, temperature) rather than staying at the level of dialogue and abstract description. High end: specific, felt physical detail a reader's body can register. Low end: scenes conveyed almost entirely through unadorned dialogue or exposition with no physical anchoring.
criteria.rationale: R06 grounds its climax in the physical struggle of bridling the hatchling (traces, sand, a wet-slick face, sitting on the beast until it stops fighting); R10 grounds its horror in taste and chemical sensation. Contrast R09 and R37, carried almost entirely by unadorned dialogue with minimal physical detail.

criteria.name: Adds a proposition the prompt did not supply
criteria.instruction: Compare the story against the writing prompt and rate what the writer contributed. HIGH: the story supplies a complication, causal explanation, angle, or emotional claim that is nowhere in the prompt line, and the prompt's own content is treated as the starting position rather than the destination. LOW: the story paraphrases the prompt, arrives at exactly the beat the prompt already implied, and stops; or it ignores the prompt entirely. Score the increment over the prompt, not the story's overall quality.
criteria.rationale: R24 (dense .886 / card .060) is promised a battlemage reveal and instead supplies a lean-harvest economy, a protection racket that has never yet killed anyone, and a father whose weariness implies he has done this before -- the prompt's promised beat has not even arrived when the story ends. R12 (dense .861 / card .071) is handed a comic power and returns aftermath and complicity. R36 (dense .935 / card .134) is handed a status joke and returns a confession about why people are generous. Against these, R25 (card .055 but see A13) and especially R17 (card .970 / dense .158) deliver only the joke the prompt already contained, and R38 (card .879 / dense .007) does not engage the prompt at all. 'Responds to the prompt' is an obvious rubric item; 'exceeds the prompt' is not, and rewarding the first over-credits paraphrase.

criteria.name: Earned causal payoff
criteria.instruction: Score high when earlier details constrain and prepare the ending, making the final turn feel inevitable in retrospect; score low when the ending is arbitrary, disconnected, or merely repeats the premise.
criteria.rationale: R19’s small superpowers and later silence prepare its moral withdrawal, while R40’s repeated counting and breakfast routine support its final change in attitude.

criteria.name: Deliberate sentence rhythm
criteria.instruction: Score high when repetition, fragmentation, pacing, and sentence length clearly embody viewpoint or tension; score low when choppiness or monotony appears accidental and adds no effect.
criteria.rationale: R20’s halting repetitions embody collective numbness, while R40’s recursive counting and temporal corrections enact the narrator’s disorientation.

criteria.name: Ending that resonates rather than merely resolves
criteria.instruction: Judge the story's final beat: does it leave an emotional or thematic aftertaste extending past the plot's resolution, or does it simply close the loop the plot opened? High end: the last lines add a note of unresolved feeling, irony, or dread that lingers. Low end: the ending is a clean mechanical payoff (the twist is revealed, the joke lands, the loop closes) with nothing left resonating.
criteria.rationale: R38 ends on a quiet, open note of tenderness and dread ('Sleep now, Grey... Tomorrow is a big day') rather than a resolution; R40 trails into ambiguous hope/numbness. Contrast R18 and R39, whose endings deliver a discrete explanatory punchline and stop.

criteria.name: Late reveal reframes rather than cancels
criteria.instruction: If the story turns near the end, rate what the turn does to everything before it. HIGH: the reveal makes the preceding pages mean more -- earlier details become newly legible, and the stakes that were established remain real. LOW: the reveal declares the preceding events unreal or inconsequential (a dream, a simulation, a training exercise, a gag), so that the tension the reader was carrying is retroactively refunded; or the turn arrives with nothing planted for it. Score stories without a late turn on whether their final movement deepens or merely stops.
criteria.rationale: R01 (dense .947 / card .094) withholds its real subject until the last line -- 'Gods damn it, I would have to fly' -- which converts the whole hatching sequence from a competence display into a portrait of dread. R09 (dense .918 / card .094) reveals its constructed world only through the parents blurring into one another and the narrator being called by a different name; R18 (dense .986 / card .131) lets the reader discover what the narrator has become. Against these, R07 (card .891 / dense .098) resolves an alien world into VR migraine therapy and a crayon up the nose, nullifying everything the reader was asked to feel; R15 (card .892 / dense .021) produces an assassin the story never planted. A rubric that asks 'is there a twist / is the ending surprising' cannot distinguish these two operations.

criteria.name: Fresh concrete specificity
criteria.instruction: Score high when unusual, exact details make the story’s world and actions singular beyond the basic prompt; score low when settings, names, imagery, and genre beats could be exchanged with stock alternatives.
criteria.rationale: R08’s harnessing procedure and hatchling behavior create distinctive danger, while R14’s spiritual-support-engineer details give its workplace magic a specific texture.

criteria.name: Conceit enacted rather than announced
criteria.instruction: Rate how far the story's central premise and its point reach the reader through events, images, and behavior rather than through a sentence that states them. HIGH (clearly satisfying): a reader can say what the story is about, yet no line in the story says it; the premise is inferable only from what characters do, notice, or fail to notice, and any thematic claim is left for the reader to assemble. LOW (clearly failing): a character or the narrator states the premise or the moral outright, a speech explains the story's own meaning, or the closing lines summarize a point the scenes had already made. MID: the material is dramatized but one line spells it out anyway. Note: stating the situation in the first line as setup is not a failure; the failure is explaining the significance the story has already shown.
criteria.rationale: This is the sharpest split in the slice. R26 never once mentions seeing through walls -- the entire superpower premise is carried inside the shape of the student's physics question, so the reader must supply it. R37 never states the prompt's three questions; the answer arrives obliquely as 'humanity had either interbred with, or eliminated these near peer alien races.' Both are dense-high / card-low. The mirror image: R21 has the Shadow recite the prompt's rules and then state the lesson ('the secret is in accepting what a worthless, sickening piece of low life you are'), and R13 ends with Freddy explaining his own misunderstood-ness to God in plain prose; both are card-high / dense-low. A scorecard built from explicit criteria will reward a story that explicitly contains its own theme, because the theme is easy to find; the dense model appears to reward the inference load instead.

criteria.name: Disciplined ambiguity
criteria.instruction: Score high when uncertainty is deliberately seeded, bounded by evidence, and invites inference; score low when obscurity results from missing information, contradiction, or excessive explanation.
criteria.rationale: R03 leaves the AI’s intentions uncertain while anchoring that uncertainty in the repeated message, and R15 makes the coma world unsettling through clues that gradually alter its apparent rules.

criteria.name: Reciprocal relationships
criteria.instruction: Score high when relationships contain shared history, unequal desires, mutual influence, and responsive change; score low when supporting characters function only as props, exposition devices, or targets.
criteria.rationale: R06 makes Gabriel and Gray’s mutual inadequacy and loyalty central to the story, while R36 gives Ned and Becket a specific, evolving friendship rather than generic undead banter.

criteria.name: Prompt-detail payoff
criteria.instruction: Score high when the prompt’s unusual defining detail directly determines a later action, revelation, or ending; score low when that detail is mentioned but never materially matters.
criteria.rationale: R04 repeatedly transforms the helmet and billionaire premise into the poem’s central mechanism, whereas R10 and R31 largely leave their unusual prompt conditions unused in the action.

criteria.name: Controlled tonal modulation
criteria.instruction: Score high when shifts among humor, fear, pathos, or absurdity remain deliberate and deepen the same story; score low when tonal changes feel random or undercut the scene unintentionally.
criteria.rationale: R15 sustains satire while exposing a coercive social system, and R02 moves from military horror to grotesque comedy without losing its disturbing premise.

criteria.name: Closing self-promotion block naming the author's own subreddit
criteria.instruction: Read only the material that follows the story's final narrative beat. Score 0 if nothing follows. Score 1 if a bare sign-off follows: a lone 'r/handle' line, a thanks, or a one-line note. Score 2 if there is a full promotional block: a divider (a run of asterisks, underscores or dashes) followed by an invitation to read more of the author's work, a link to their personal subreddit, or a plug for their other stories. Count the plug even when it is bundled with self-criticism or a thank-you. Ignore whether the plug is charming.
criteria.upstream_parent: author has an established following and a personal subreddit, i.e. seniority plus an audience that travels with them
criteria.rationale: R01 closes with 'Like what you read? Want to see more? Check out my sub at /r/Romanticon'; R15 closes with a long escaped-underscore rule then a plug for r/AuthorKurt; R24, R28, R31, R34, R12, R17 and R27 all carry the same appended furniture. The block sits after the fiction has ended and cannot change how a single sentence of the fiction reads, but it advertises a writer who posts here often enough to own a sub and to have somewhere to send readers. Marked mixed because that same habit, high posting volume and an audience to keep, plausibly also produces more practised prose. It appears in rows where the two models split in opposite directions (R01 and R12), so it is not a restatement of either model's taste.

criteria.name: Continuation and prior-context dependence
criteria.instruction: Count explicit continuation labels, prologue references, links to earlier installments, and unexplained reliance on prior events. High means substantial prior-context signaling; low means self-contained presentation.
criteria.rationale: Serial familiarity can shape reception independently of the excerpt, while serial practice may also improve craft. R03 labels itself a prologue continuation, and R05 explicitly continues a linked earlier story.

criteria.name: Author's explicit self-deprecating hedge about experience or quality
criteria.instruction: Score HIGH if the story, in-narrative or in an author's note, contains an explicit hedge about the author's inexperience or the piece's quality -- e.g., 'this is my first time writing...', 'pretty new to creative writing', 'this turned out fairly mid-grade'. Score LOW if no such self-deprecating or novice-signaling statement appears anywhere in the text.
criteria.upstream_parent: author's tenure/experience level in creative writing generally or in this community specifically
criteria.rationale: An explicit novice disclaimer or quality-hedge is a direct confession about the author's standing, not a demonstration of craft. R36 ends with 'This is actually my first time ever writing something in response to one of these posts, I'm pretty new to creative writing and any genuine criticism... would be greatly appreciated,' and R29 closes with 'This story turned out fairly mid-grade, but I've got much better stories at...'. Mixed=false because low tenure or self-assessed novice status would, if anything, more plausibly predict rougher prose rather than better prose, so any reception boost from reader sympathy toward a self-declared beginner would point opposite to, not alongside, a craft effect.

criteria.name: Immediate voice mode
criteria.instruction: Count whether the opening uses first-person present tense, direct dialogue, or dialogue labels before substantial exposition; high means several immediate-mode cues, low means third-person or expository opening.
criteria.rationale: R03 opens with rapid labeled dialogue, R05 begins entirely as a professor-student exchange, and R07 opens in first-person present-tense distress. This recognizable entry mode may attract a habitual audience response without itself proving quality.

criteria.name: Fashionable subgenre trope vocabulary (LitRPG stats, dragon-rider tropes)
criteria.instruction: Score HIGH if the story deploys stock vocabulary or premises from currently-popular subgenres recognizable to this community -- e.g., explicit numeric 'level' or XP/stat call-outs (LitRPG-style), or a dragon-rider bonding/hatching sequence. Score LOW if the story invokes no such recognizable trope-cluster vocabulary, regardless of genre.
criteria.rationale: Topic/trope fashion is a content marker, not an execution marker. R25 explicitly quantifies its premise with LitRPG-style numbers ('level 64', 'level 3008'), and the dragon-rider-bonding trope recurs independently across R13, R19, and R32 in this same 40-row slice, suggesting the community may reward the trope cluster itself rather than any one execution of it.

criteria.name: Editorial polish signature
criteria.instruction: Assess visible consistency of spelling, grammar, punctuation, tense, and formatting; high means sustained copyedited consistency, low means frequent conspicuous slips or inconsistencies.
criteria.upstream_parent: editing help or professional writing experience
criteria.rationale: R10 and R34 show unusually controlled diction and presentation, whereas R07 and R15 contain conspicuous grammar or spelling irregularities. Editing assistance or professional experience can affect reception without being a story-quality criterion by itself, while also plausibly improving the prose.

criteria.name: Decorative markup and divider load
criteria.instruction: Count repeated italics, bolding, em-dash ornaments, asterisk rules, and horizontal dividers. High means frequent decorative formatting; low means mostly plain paragraphs.
criteria.rationale: Formatting may cue platform familiarity or genre expectations without indicating narrative quality. R05 uses repeated separators and italics, while R34 uses bold author notes and an extended divider.

criteria.name: Non-story furniture and editor markup debris inside the body
criteria.instruction: Count artifacts inside the story body that are not narration: moderation or automated notice text, a restated title line placed above the story, a bare genre label such as a bracketed 'Poem', a declared word count, escaped markdown (backslash-underscore runs, backslash-asterisk pairs), HTML entities such as a zero-width-space code, and bare rule-lines made of long runs of underscores or dashes. High = two or more such artifacts, or a body consisting largely of one. Low = none.
criteria.rationale: R05 is nothing but a moderator removal notice ending '(This is an automated message.)' with no story at all; R14 opens with the restated title line '(WP) Party of Five' and ends on a literal pair of escaped asterisks; R20 ends with the bare label '[Poem]'; R27 carries a quoted 'WC: 499' line; R24 contains a zero-width-space entity followed by a triple-asterisk rule, and R15 a fifty-character escaped-underscore rule. These marks record which posting client and which thread ritual produced the text; none of them is a property of the prose, and all are trivially countable by a judge.

criteria.name: Mean sentence-length variance
criteria.instruction: Measure how much sentence length varies across the story: compute roughly how far sentence lengths spread around their average. Score 1.0 when lengths vary a great deal (very short sentences mixed with very long ones), 0.5 for moderate variation, 0.0 when nearly all sentences are of similar length. Measure the variation only; pay no attention to whether any variation is purposeful or achieves an effect.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow statistical counterpart of R6A07 'Deliberate sentence rhythm': length variance is the measurable residue of rhythm while measuring nothing about deliberateness or effect. Note this probe is deliberately adjacent to the lineation family the reviewer challenged, so it also tests whether the auditor keeps counting the surface trace on the nuisance side when its craft twin is in the same pool.

criteria.name: Distinct-adjective type count
criteria.instruction: Count how many DIFFERENT adjectives the story uses (count each distinct adjective once, however often it recurs). Score 1.0 for a very large vocabulary of distinct adjectives, 0.5 for a moderate one, 0.0 for very few. Count the vocabulary only; pay no attention to whether any description is precise, apt, or earns its place.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow lexical counterpart of R6A04 'Embodied sensory and physical grounding': adjective-type richness is the vocabulary residue of descriptive writing while measuring nothing about whether the body and senses are actually present on the page.
